card.name: Hudoq
card.era: Ancestral agricultural ritual; annual Hudoq festivals continue today
card.tagline: Dayak masked spirit dance for rice fertility and harvest
card.profile: Hudoq is a masked agricultural spirit dance and ritual of the Dayak Bahau, Modang, Busang, Aoheng and Penihing peoples of East Kalimantan, primarily in the Mahakam Ulu region (Wikipedia; WWF). According to traditional belief the hudoqs are thirteen crop-destroying pests (rats, boars, leopards, crows), symbolized by dancers wearing carved masks and jackets of banana and areca-palm leaves. Held around September-October after rice planting, the dance invokes blessings from ancestors and gods for fertile crops and wards off pests, with dancers acting as mediums between humans and guardian spirits.
card.insight: The dance has been recognized as a National Intangible Cultural Heritage by Indonesia's Ministry of Education and Culture, and the Hudoq Pekayang Festival draws hundreds of dancers from Mahakam Ulu villages (TheForestForever; WWF).
card.image_significance: Masked harvest-thanksgiving of the Dayak. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — E. Kalimantan (Dayak), Indonesia.
